abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Using a cohort of 893 adults who underwent medical check-ups with rich data collection across diet, lifestyle, clinical labs, cardiac stress testing, and microbiome profiling, we show that a gut microbial health index (MHI), originally defined using a large meta-analysis of various human disease cohorts, is also substantially associated with lifestyle and diet. This association persists across the overall cohort, disease-free subsets, and individuals with common medical conditions such as hypertension and dyslipidemia. The gut MHI was positively correlated with factors such as variation in cardiac stress test fitness, fiber intake, and well-being, and negatively correlated with exposure to ultra-processed foods and markers of subclinical inflammation (WBC and CRP mostly within normal limits). Lipidomics profiling of a subcohort revealed that triglycerides correlate positively with ultraprocessed foods, and negatively with unsaturated fats, olive oil, and nuts, linking diet, MHI, and lipid profile. Estimating the contribution of modifiable dietary and lifestyle factors to the MHI uncovers actionable ways to improve or worsen the personal MHI. Analyses of previously published intervention studies showed that the MHI responds quickly to dietary changes, within the predicted range. Our findings emphasize the potential of using microbiomes, and specifically the MHI, as a reporter of overall health.

sec.title: Background
sec.p:
The rapid increase in the incidence and prevalence of modern diseases, such as obesity, metabolic disorders, diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, and colon cancer among young adults, is believed to be closely associated with lifestyle factors, industrialization, urbanization, and exposure to a Westernized diet, rather than with genetic changes, which typically occur over several generations. The impact of the changing environment on the microbiome is especially notable when comparing industrialized and more rural communities. 1
,
2 The environment, 3
,
4 including diet, 5‐8 significantly influences the personal gut microbiome and is linked to predisposition to or protection from various diseases. 8‐10 The identification of modifiable factors that may reverse the microbial shifts, and potential composite microbial biomarker that can capture them, may direct recommendations that can impact health and potentially attenuate the increase in the prevalence of some modern-era diseases.

The human gut microbiome is an integral part of the human ecosystem, interacting with human exposures, 11 and positioning it as a potential general tool to assess health and host exposures across diverse health-related dimensions. Support for this concept arises from several systematic comparisons of independent studies that identify shared bacterial signal patterns across different diseases. 10
,
12
,
13 We, for example, previously identified predominant shared microbial responses across cohorts of various diseases 12 to compose a per-sample microbial health index (MHI) tool, which was successfully applied in subsequent analyses involving independent disease cohorts. 1
,
14 However, in most of these studies, the focus was on diseases, as we and others lacked detailed information regarding lifestyle and dietary exposures, and mostly focused on specific disease vs. control comparisons. Here, we thoroughly analyzed 893 participants who underwent routine annual Executive Medical Checkups at a tertiary medical center. Data acquisition included reports from the hospital electronic medical records (EMR), lab tests, ICD-10 disease codes, prescribed Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) medication classes, cardiac stress test ergometry (Bruce protocol), and participants filled out detailed lifestyle and food frequency questionnaires. 16S sequencing (V4) was used to determine the fecal microbial composition, and we calculated per-participant microbial indices. We aimed to determine the effects of interactions between exposure, diet, and lifestyle on frequent health-related conditions, and assess whether gut microbial indices, similar to measuring fever and blood pressure, can be used as a composite general tool to evaluate health across physical, mental, medical, and well-being dimensions.

sec.title: Cohort characteristics
sec.p:
We analyzed 893 participants who underwent annual Executive Medical Checkups (61% male, mean age 57 ± 11 y, median BMI of 25, and 10% smokers), who submitted fecal samples (Table 1, Figure 1A, Dataset S1). The most prevalent medical conditions among participants were metabolic syndrome (37%), dyslipidemia requiring lipid-modifying medications (22%), prediabetes and diabetes based on HbA1c levels > = 5.7 (19%), and documented hypertension (17%, full list in Dataset S1). Clinical parameters included cardiac stress test ergometry, available for 798 subjects, including METs scores, which provide a standardized measure of a person's exercise capacity, with higher levels indicating improved fitness. Clinical lab results, available for 846 subjects, included fasting lipid profiles, chemistry, blood vitamin levels, and complete blood counts. The lifestyle questionnaire included questions about bowel movements, alcohol consumption, coffee intake, and intake of vitamin/mineral supplements. A comprehensive Food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) was uniformly applied. 15
,
16 Adherence to the Mediterranean diet was assessed using the MEDAS 17 (Mediterranean Diet Adherence Screener) score, with higher scores indicating better adherence (median MEDAS score of 10, IQR 9–12). NOVA class 4 exposure to ultra-processed foods and beverages, as a percentage of food items, was reported with a median percentage among participants being 23% (IQR 18%–29%). Sixty-seven percent of the participants (491 out of 728) reported being satisfied or very satisfied with their general condition, which was indicative of overall well-being. We composed lifestyle-based and EMR-based indices (see methods) that summarize related phenotypes. The lifestyle index includes diet, exercise, etc., and the EMR-based index is based on lab results, diseases, and medications.

fn.p: *Disease full list and frequency in Dataset S1.
For the analyses, we used a gender-normalized z-score of the METs values to account for known gender differences.
Samples within 4 weeks of antibiotic exposure were excluded.

sec.p: Stratifying the cohort by age quartiles (Q4 representing the older subgroup), gender, and the presence or absence of diseases revealed (Figure 1B–D) that older participants tended to practice healthier lifestyles, as evidenced by higher MEDAS scores and lower exposure to NOVA 4 ultraprocessed foods, along with a higher overall lifestyle index, and reported higher levels of well-being satisfaction (Figure 1B, Mann‒Whitney p < 0.05). However, as expected, the older group had lower EMR health indices, as those accumulate with increasing age, and reduced exercise capacity, as indicated by their METs scores. Participants with and without diseases differed in their EMR-based index, as anticipated, and in their ergometry METs. Gender differences showed that males consumed a larger proportion of NOVA 4 ultraprocessed food, experienced more frequent bowel movements, and reported greater well-being satisfaction (Figure 1D, Table 1). We evaluated the dietary and lifestyle datasets and tested correlations between blood levels of specific clinical vitamins, including folic acid, vitamins B12 and D, and their corresponding oral supplementation vs. dietary intake. This revealed that blood folate levels were more strongly related to dietary intake (Spearman r = 0.32, p = 3.4E-8); vitamin B12 correlated with both supplementation and dietary intake (Spearman r = 0.13–14, p < 3E-03); and blood vitamin D levels were associated with supplementation rather than diet (Spearman r = 0.2, p = 4.3E-05, Figure 1E).

sec.title: Fewer healthy blood lipid profiles are positively associated with the consumption of carbohydrates and ultraprocessed foods
sec.p: PCA was used to capture dietary patterns (Figure 2A). The dominant factors contributing to separation on PC1 included fiber consumption, dietary folate, and other vitamin consumption in the diet, with modest differences related to gender on PC1 (p = 0.03). Factors contributing to PC2 were linked to protein and saturated fat consumption compared to carbohydrate consumption (Figure 2A). Clinical measurement of lipid profiles is part of routine evaluation in adult checkups, and it is used to screen for and assess the risk of cardiovascular diseases, such as heart attacks and strokes. To link dietary exposure and clinical lab lipid profiles results, we identified positive and significant positive correlations between rates of NOVA class 4 ultraprocessed foods and beverages, added sugar, and gender normalized BMI, with blood triglyceride levels, with a negative correlation with HDL (Figure 2B; full correlations are shown in Figure S1). Triglyceride levels were also positively correlated with white blood cell (WBC) and neutrophil counts, which were mostly within normal limits. Additionally, both LDL cholesterol and triglycerides showed a positive correlation with C-reactive protein (CRP), which was mostly within the normal range (Table 1). Conversely, higher cardiac stress test ergometry METs, an objective measurement of improved fitness, and adherence to a Mediterranean diet, nut consumption, a diet high in fat and low in carbohydrates, and olive oil intake exhibited a negative correlation with clinical blood triglyceride levels.

sec.p: To enhance analysis beyond standard clinical lipid profile tests, we subjected blood samples from 62 females not taking lipid-lowering medications to lipidomics (details in Dataset S2). Highlighted correlation for this subset with the clinical laboratory lipids (Figure S1B) showed overall comparable patterns as those in the overall cohort (Figure 2B). Lipidomics data comprising 816 lipids, categorized into different lipid classes (Figure 2C), and saturated and unsaturated fatty acids (Figure 2D), were correlated with EMR data, laboratory results, dietary habits, and lifestyle factors. We present metadata fields, stratified into specific data types, with at least one significant correlation to the lipids (see methods and Dataset S2 for specific statistical details). A large fraction of lipids correlated with the clinical lab triglyceride levels (Figure 2C) and LDL cholesterol, but several others did not, highlighting variations among measured lipids beyond traditional clinical lipid measurements. Correlations and clusters of lipids were noted with dietary intake of added sugar, the consumption of higher NOVA class 4 ultraprocessed foods and beverages, saturated fat, and carbohydrate intake. Conversely, blood lipid profiles demonstrated negative correlations with the consumption of vegetables and fiber, as well as vitamins E, folate, and several minerals, such as dietary copper and magnesium, and with the ergometry METs score. Notably, negative correlations were also observed between blood lipids and the dietary consumption of oils and oil-rich products, such as olive oil, nuts, omega-6 fatty acids, and monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFA lipids). We observed additional lipid clusters that were linked with the consumption of proteins, mainly from fish and food items rich in vitamin D, B vitamins (including B3, B6, B7, and B12), and omega-3 fatty acids. These features correlated with a specific cluster of triglycerides, diglycerides, as well as phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and phosphatidylcholine (PC), which are essential phospholipids found in cell membranes. We observed correlation patterns upon categorizing fatty acids into saturated fats, which have carbon chains with no double bonds and are considered less healthy (zero C = C double bonds), and unsaturated fats, which contain at least one C = C double bond in their fatty acid chains. The unsaturated fats were further analyzed based on the number of double bonds present (Figure 2D). These analyses highlight correlations between specific dietary exposures and less healthy lipid profiles, higher blood triglyceride and LDL cholesterol levels, and lower HDL levels.

sec.title: The gut microbiome serves as a biomarker of health across various dimensions, both in healthy individuals and those with common medical conditions
sec.p:
A permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) was performed to evaluate the impact of different factors on the overall variation in the gut microbiome. The top five features in each category demonstrate that lifestyle and diet explain more variance than diseases and medications (Figure 3A). Next, we used MaAsLin2 (multivariable association with linear models), building models for each metadata feature against the relative abundances of all ASVs, controlling for age, gender, and BMI. Only features and ASVs with at least one significant association, with FDR < 0.1 across all pairs (Figure 3B & Dataset S1, summarizing all associations), are shown. We identified two main clusters: one linked with healthier patterns, higher lifestyle and medical indices, better physical fitness as indicated by higher METs on the cardiac stress test, increased fiber intake, MEDAS, and vegetable consumption, and a second cluster associated with exposure to more medications, smoking, sugary drinks, salty snacks, and added sugars; and higher intake of NOVA class 4 ultraprocessed foods and beverages. Most signals correlated with a broader microbial community rather than with specific taxa, as shown in these analyses and confirmed by a complementary HAllA (hierarchical all-against-all associations) method (Figure S2). However, we were able to replicate previously identified associations, such as the link between more frequent coffee consumption and the Lawsonibacter asaccharolyticus,
18 along with other taxa (Figure 3B & S2). Interestingly, we also observed a notable link between added sugar intake and bacteria typically found in the oral cavity [i.e., Haemophiles (ASVs 6349 & 6380), Streptococcus (ASVs 12252 & 12303), and Villanella (ASV 13187) taxa], which were detected in feces (Figure S2). Our previous work defined a microbial health index (MHI), based on data from 12,838 subjects across 59 disease cohorts, 12 including conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease, depression, diabetes, Parkinson’s disease, autism, and others, spanning regions such as America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. This index reveals a shared microbial signature across many diseases. The MHI is calculated using the log ratio of health-associated to disease-associated bacterial amplicon sequence variants (97 and 31 ASVs, respectively, Dataset S1). Above the heatmap (Figure 3C), we marked the ASVs included in the MHI based on our previous analyses, 12 showing significant (Chi-square p = 0.001) enrichment of health-associated ASVs in cluster 1 (blue) and disease-associated ASVs in cluster 2 (red).

sec.p: To further test the applicability of the MHI, where higher values indicate a healthier, or less disease-related microbiome, in this cohort, we examined its associations with diet, exposures, and EMR data among participants undergoing routine checkups, representing aging adults in westernized regions. We then defined correlations between composite dietary exposures to the Mediterranean diet and ultraprocessed foods, lifestyle and EMR medical index, with the MHI, and the more commonly used Faith pd alpha diversity. Significant negative correlations were observed between the gut MHI and the consumption of NOVA class 4 ultraprocessed foods and beverages (r = −0.13, p = 4.9e-4). In contrast, positive correlations were found between the gut MHI and MEDAS (r = 0.16, p = 1.7e-5), an overall healthier lifestyle index (r = 0.17, p = 5.3e-7), and a healthier EMR-based index (r = 0.15, p = 8e-6). Similar trends were noted with Faith’s phylogenetic diversity 19 ; however, most Spearman's correlation coefficients were weaker, and the p-values were less significant in these analyses (r = −0.11 & p = 2.3e-3 with NOVA, r = 0.07 & p = 5e-2 for MEDAS, r = 0.1& p = 3.8e-3 for healthier lifestyle index, and r = 0.09 & p = 9.9e-3 for healthier EMR-based), compared to the correlations observed with the MHI. Individuals with healthier lifestyle indexes exhibited a higher MHI also when looking at specific subsets; among participants without EMR-recorded medical conditions, within the older subgroup (Q4), and in subjects with hypertension or metabolic syndrome (Figure 3C), indicating a strong connection between lifestyle choices and microbial health, even among individuals with underlying medical conditions and older adults.

Expanding this analysis and demonstrating correlations across various features, categorized into basic characteristics, diet, lifestyle, ergometry stress tests, lab results, diseases, and medication (Figure 3D), whereby the green color indicates a healthier MHI and greater diversity, and the red color shows overall negative correlations linked to a lower MHI and diversity. Key findings indicate that healthier dietary habits, such as higher intakes of fiber, vegetables, fruits, and nuts, along with overall adherence to the Mediterranean diet, are associated with a higher MHI and diversity. This pattern remains consistent across all subject subgroups; when separating the subjects based on sex, and when including those with specified medical conditions, including subjects with metabolic syndrome, those on lipid-modifying agents, individuals with prediabetes and diabetes, and those with hypertension. Conversely, increased consumption of NOVA class 4 ultraprocessed foods and beverages, red processed meat, added sugars, and savory bakery products correlates with a lower microbial health index. Furthermore, the frequency of bowel movements, an indirect measure of gut transit time, and blood levels of vitamin B12 were the only features showing a significant inverse correlation between the MHI and Faith diversity. More frequent bowel movements were positively associated with a higher MHI and lower Faith diversity. The stress test ergometry METs score, which measures exercise intensity and fitness in a standardized way, was positively correlated with a higher microbial health index. Elevated blood triglycerides (TG), white blood cells (WBC), neutrophils, and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels were negatively correlated with healthier microbial indices. Additionally, certain diseases and medications are associated with lower microbial health indices. Interestingly, a family history of ischemic disease was linked to improved microbial health indices, potentially suggesting an improved lifestyle overall in this at-risk population. Sensitivity analyses that stratified the cohort into subjects recruited during 2022–2023 (n = 447) and 2024–2025 (n = 446) revealed overall similar patterns (Table S1 and Figure S3), which likely reduced the possibility of dominant confounders.

sec.title: Regression models highlight modifiable exposures linked with improved microbial health index
sec.p: We used logistic regression modeling that accounted for age, gender, and both lifestyle-based and electronic medical record (EMR) indices (see Methods). We systematically evaluated potential modifiable factors, such as diet, lifestyle, and stress test ergometry results, that are linked with higher MHI values (Figure 4). The plots display significant features along with their regression coefficients and 95% confidence intervals (CI, Figure 4A), and the required change for a 0.5-point improvement in the microbial health index. For example, increasing fruit or vegetable intake by three servings a day is associated with a 0.5-point increase in the microbial health index, while reducing red and processed meat consumption from daily to zero or once weekly is linked to a similar improvement. The model (Figure 4A) was analyzed using all participants and specifically among the oldest 25% of the population, as well as those without documented diseases, subjects with metabolic syndrome, patients on lipid-modifying agents, individuals with prediabetes and diabetes, and those with hypertension. The trends observed were consistent across different groups, suggesting that modifiable factors can lead to improved health-related microbial signals even when applied to individuals with various medical conditions and an aging population.

sec.p:
To further support that the change in MHI following the dietary intervention matches the predicted direction and magnitude obtained via the regression in our cohort, the MHI was computed using previously published raw datasets from an independent dietary intervention dataset from two separate studies involving participants from the U.S. 5
,
20 One study utilized a crossover-controlled feeding design with two different dietary interventions. 20 Both dietary interventions contained the same total energy and macronutrient proportions: carbohydrates (55.0%), protein (30.0%), and fat (15.0%). However, the diets differed in terms of glycemic load and dietary fiber. This distinction was primarily achieved by increasing the consumption of whole fruits in Diet A (low fiber) from 0.8 portions to 2.4 portions in Diet B (high fiber), along with increasing vegetable intake from 3.8 portions to 4.7 portions (Figure 4B). Additionally, Diet B involved a reduction in animal protein by 11 g, which was offset by an increase in both plant-based and seafood protein by the same amount. Consistent with our model, the median MHI for Diet B was 0.7 points higher than that of Diet A, with median values of 8.2 for Diet A and 8.9 for Diet B, and mean values of 7.7 for Diet A and 8.4 for Diet B. This is illustrated per participant (Figure 4C) and by diet type (Figure 4D). In the second interventional dietary study, 5 participants were exposed to a predominant animal-based diet. Calculating the MHI daily before, during, and after the 4-day exposures, we observed a rapid within-2-day reduction in the MHI upon exposure to this unhealthy diet rich in animal-based proteins from their baseline (Figure 4E), indicating a dynamic effect on the MHI. We included the US cohorts as examples of a dietary intervention, using the MHI, to imply that modifiable factors such as diet as interventions are instrumental to improve the MHI.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The microbial health index (MHI), which is based on bacteria known to respond to multiple diseases, has now been demonstrated to reflect lifestyle and nutritional behavior, even when accounting for existing medical conditions in the overall cohort, but also in those without documented medical conditions, and within individuals with common medical conditions such as hypertension, dyslipidemia, and metabolic syndrome. This suggests that the same bacteria may be involved in both disease and lifestyle-related effects, indicating that these bacteria likely respond to the host's exposures and conditions rather than causing the health issues themselves. While some bacteria that directly affect disease processes, identifying them requires considering this shared response in the analysis. Additionally, quantifying personal modifiable lifestyles and nutritional practices that contribute to better or worse MHI and supporting the ability to affect the MHI using available interventional studies, suggests that the MHI could serve as a holistic marker of overall health, reflect lifestyle choices and medical conditions, and can be used to monitor personal changes over a relatively short time frame of several days to weeks.

Our cohort design offers advantages over previous studies. The participants did not have major illnesses but rather exhibited common age-related medical conditions. We included individuals attending annual executive medical checkups at a tertiary center, who, in addition to capturing information from reliable electronic medical record (EMR) data with ICD-10 medical conditions, ATC3 classified prescribed medications, clinical lab, and cardiac stress test ergometry, also completed a comprehensive and detailed dietary exposure questionnaire that provides information on food group servings, micronutrients, macronutrients, adherence to the Mediterranean diet, and exposure to ultra-processed foods. Additionally, collecting fecal samples allowed us to characterize the microbial community, calculating various microbial indices, including a previously developed MHI. Although the MHI is based on previous analysis of disease cohorts, when applying it to samples from this cohort of subjects attending routine checkups, we observed strong correlations between this index and various lifestyle and diet habits, as well as health, fitness, and overall well-being. Faith alpha diversity showed weaker correlations with overall similar trends in most parameters when compared with the microbial health index, suggesting superior performance of the microbial index. Complementing previous findings, we showed that adherence to the Mediterranean diet, fiber intake, and reduced exposure to ultra-processed food are associated with changes in the microbial health index. Furthermore, we connected this microbial index to the levels of WBC, CRP, and cardiac stress test ergometry metabolic equivalents (METs), which have been less frequently noted in prior research. Our findings suggest that an overall healthier lifestyle, characterized by a diet rich in adherence to the Mediterranean diet, olive oil, fiber, and nuts, is associated with improved laboratory results, with a healthier blood lipid profile, and positive correlations with a higher microbial health index. In contrast, we noted a persistent negative correlation between the rate of exposure to NOVA class 4 ultraprocessed foods and the MHI among individuals, regardless of medical conditions, with higher exposure among males and younger adults. Additionally, there was a positive correlation between higher exposure to ultra-processed foods and elevated triglycerides and blood unsaturated fatty acids, which was also corroborated by the lipidomics analysis. Using regression models, we highlight modifiable factors that can be implemented to modify it, showing their potential effects in two independent intervention cohorts, implying its potential to track changes; however, these predictions from an observational study require further prospective testing. Our study includes several limitations. While we report associations consistent across various sub-analyses and stratifications, causality must be formally established through appropriate study designs. While the NOVA classification is a strong indicator of diet quality and associated health outcomes, 21
,
22 there is inherent uncertainty in classifying some food items when exact processing methods are unknown. Our executive checkup cohort may be healthier and more affluent than the general population, as evidenced by a median BMI of 25 and a smoking rate of 10%. However, this homogeneity can also be viewed as a strength, as it allows us to identify dietary and lifestyle exposures linked to common medical conditions in Westernized countries, as well as signals within individuals who do not exhibit notable deleterious medical conditions, which could indicate a premedical state. This cohort belongs to a relatively high socioeconomic status, which may also shape the observed associations, and it is likely generalizable to a broader population of adults in a similar age group with a relatively healthy BMI of 25 and a low smoking rate of 10% in developed countries. Additionally, all exposures and clinical tests were measured at only a single time point, limiting our ability to capture changes over time. Furthermore, we focused solely on linear associations, and future research utilizing non-linear models may enhance some of our findings.

Declining health is noted amidst advancements in healthcare in Westernized countries, 23 and is connected to environmental and nutritional exposures. The consumption of ultra-processed foods, specifically, is linked to an increased risk of noncommunicable diseases in industrialized nations such as the UK, the US, and across Europe, 24‐26 and with a decrease in microbial diversity, lower levels of beneficial bacteria, and an expansion of pro-inflammatory ones. 27 A study based on the UK Biobank dataset found that polygenic risk scores for 22 major diseases accounted for less than 2 percentage points of variation in mortality, while environmental factors contributed 17 additional percentage points. 28 Data from the Nurses’ Health Study indicated that dietary patterns rich in plant-based foods and moderately inclusive of animal-based foods are associated with better odds of healthy aging. 9 The ISRCTN trial revealed that a transition from African heritage diets to Western-style diets impacted metabolic pathways linked to noncommunicable diseases. 11 Consequently, this highlights the importance of interventions that focus on environmental factors, as the most effective strategy to improve health. A personalized health indicator tool that reflects exposures and lifestyle may help direct and assess dietary recommendations for better implementation on a personal level. By employing a regression model that incorporates lifestyle and medical information alongside age and gender, we determine how much each specific modifiable factor is associated with an increase in MHI. The potential of this model was demonstrated by implementing the MHI in a previously published crossover dietary intervention study involving American adults, 20 which showed that participants increased their MHI following dietary modifications aligned with our model's predictions. Conversely, when applying our MHI to another intervention study 5 involving exposure to an enriched animal-based diet, we observed a rapid decline in the MHI. This relatively rapid response, within a few days, and the ability of the MHI to capture the directionality of the response toward a better or worse MHI, indicate the potential use of our model and MHI for assessing different interventions on a personal level. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines health as a complex concept, as "a state of physical, mental, and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease." With the observed association between the gut microbial composition (and specifically the MHI) and the set of factors spanning diet, lifestyle, fitness, well-being satisfaction, and medical conditions, it may serve as an additional, complementary, distinct, and convenient health reporter.

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p: The study was approved by the ethics committees at the Sheba Medical Center. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Individuals who were scheduled for their annual Executive Medical Checkups between 12/2022 and 05/2025 and agreed to participate were included. An invitation to participate in the study was sent in advance of the planned visit. Those interested filled out a form agreeing to receive a fecal collection kit, including an iced pack in a cooler container. They were instructed to collect feces and freeze the samples just before the visit or a day before the visit. On the day of the visit, the fecal samples were immediately transferred from the iced cooler to −80 by the research team. Fecal samples collected within four weeks of antibiotic use were excluded. Data collection included electronic medical records (EMR) regarding ICD-10 disease codes, Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) medication classes, clinical lab tests, and cardiac stress test results (Bruce protocol) done during the annual visit. For clinical features having different gender-related normal references, values were z-score normalized within each gender. Additionally, participants completed a Food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) and a lifestyle questionnaire that covered various dimensions, including physical, medical, habits, and general well-being. Data fields were categorized into diet, lifestyle, disease, medications, labs, etc. (Datasets S1).

sec.title: Dietary questionnaires
sec.p:
A comprehensive, validated computerized food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) was uniformly applied. 15
,
16 The FFQ output calculates the average daily nutrient content of an individual subject's diet, including macro and micronutrients, and food item servings, based on a database that was generated and validated by the Gertner Institute for Epidemiology and Health Policy Research. It combines data from BINAT (https://data.gov.il/dataset/nutrition-database), and is supplemented with data from international sources (primarily USDA, https://fdc.nal.usda.gov), and from Gertner’s food database, food composition tables, local manufacturers, and representative local recipes. 29 The NOVA classification of food/beverage level of processing is based on the work done by the ICDC MABAT team in 2019. The NOVA classification key 30
,
31 was applied, where class 4 includes ultra-processed food and drink products, and we report the percentage of items classified as NOVA 4 that a subject consumed out of the total consumed items 8 by this subject. Adherence to the Mediterranean diet was assessed using the MEDAS, 17 ranging from 0 to 14, with higher scores indicating better adherence. In the FFQ used, we included 344 food items from a wider list of 600 items, prioritizing foods and beverages that accounted for at least 80% of the total energy intake and the between-person variance in previously collected dietary intake data from the adult Israeli population. 15
,
16 Participants were asked about their intake in the previous month. FFQs reporting a daily water consumption of less than 500 g or a caloric intake below 800 kcal were excluded. The dietary data were normalized to daily 1,000 kcal caloric intake, and all FFQ variables with values over 5 standard deviations from the mean were trimmed to exactly 5 standard deviations from the mean to avoid extreme values driving the analysis. Highly correlated dietary features, with Spearman correlation values over 0.8, were merged into a single summary feature calculated as their z-score to avoid bias and improve FDR (Supplementary Dataset 1). Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed to summarize FFQ variation using the R prcomp function (utilizing standardized Euclidean distances), with the data scaled to have a mean of zero and centered to have unit variance with a standard deviation of 1. By scaling the data, we ensure that all pre-processed dietary variables contributed equally regardless of their absolute scales. The top 10 largest combined absolute scaled loadings were overlaid as arrows to visualize the contributions of the original variables to the principal components.

sec.title: Lifestyle and EMR indices
sec.p: We defined indices for this study based on the log of the ratio of the sum of quartile-normalized healthy to unhealthy lifestyles and electronic medical records (EMR) factors. For the EMR-based index, we used the values of hemoglobin (Hgb) and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels, as well as metabolic equivalent tasks (METs) from an ergometry stress test in the numerator. This was divided by resting pulse rates from the ergometry stress test, triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) levels, HbA1c results, the number of documented ICD-10 diseases, the number of recorded medications classified by the ATC system, body mass index (BMI) normalized by gender, and results from intraocular pressure measurements using the eye puff test in the denominator. EMR = Hgb + HDL + METs/Pulse + Triglycerides + LDL + HbA1c + nDisease + nMedication + BMI + EyePuff.

For the lifestyle-based index, the numerator included values for mean daily steps, hours of nighttime sleep, home cooking versus eating out, frequency of physical activity, intake of fiber, whole grains, fruits, vegetables, olive oil, and fish servings, as well as MEDAS. In the denominator, we included smoking, saturated and trans fatty acids, added sugars, consumption of red and processed meat, sugary drinks, sweet and savory baked goods, and the fraction of NOVA class 4 ultraprocessed foods and drinks (out of the total personal diet items). LifeStyle = Steps + Sleep + Cooking + PhysActivity + Fibers + WholeGrains + Fruits + Vegetables + OliveOil + Fish + MEDAS/Smoking + SatFat + TransFat + AddedSugar + Meat + SugarDrinks + SweetBake + SavoryBake + NOVA4.

sec.title: 16S rRNA sequencing
sec.p:
Fecal DNA extraction and PCR amplification of the variable region 4 (V4) of the 16S rRNA gene using Illumina-adapted universal primers 515F/806R were conducted using the direct PCR protocol [Extract-N-Amp Plant PCR kit (Sigma–Aldrich, Inc.)], 14,32‐37 and sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq platform. Reads were processed in a data curation pipeline implemented in QIIME 2 version 2023.7. 38
,
39 Quality control was performed by truncating reads after three consecutive Phred scores lower than 20. Reads with ambiguous base calls or shorter than 150 bp after quality truncation were discarded. Amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) detection was performed using Deblur, 40 resulting in 893 samples with a median of 23522 reads/sample (IQR 1407–35822). ASVs present in less than 1% of the samples were removed. Additionally, candidate contaminant ASVs were filtered using dbBact 41 by removing ASVs with the f-score mean for (“water”, “soil”, and “mus musculus”) higher than “homo sapiens”, resulting in 2845 ASVs after filtering. ASV taxonomy was assigned using the Greengenes2 (2022.10) database. Assignments were first attempted via exact sequence matching. For ASVs without an exact match, a naive Bayes classifier pre-trained on the Greengenes2 (2022.10) database was utilized for classification. All samples were then rarefied to 4k reads for α- and β-diversity analysis. Faith’s phylogenetic diversity 19 was used as a measure of within-sample α diversity, and unweighted UniFrac was used as a measure of between-sample β-diversity, 42 using a phylogenetic tree generated by SATé-enabled phylogenetic placement (SEPP). 43 The resulting distance matrix was used to perform a principal coordinate analysis (PCoA). Health index: The per-sample microbial health index (MHI) was calculated as previously described 12 for each sample; the log of the ratio of the frequency sum of previously identified health-associated ASVs bacteria (97) to disease-associated ASVs bacteria (31) was calculated and defined as the MHI (with higher values indicating a better health-associated microbiome). The complete list of ASVs used for the health index calculation is listed in Dataset S1. Quantifications of variance were calculated using PERMANOVA with the adonis2 function in the R package Vegan, 25 on the rarefied unweighted UniFrac distance values. The total variance explained by each variable was calculated while accounting for age and gender, and was calculated independently for each group/subgroup and feature. To identify associations between microbial taxa and host metadata, we employed MaAsLin2 (Multivariable Association with Linear Models, R package version 1.8.0). Individual models were constructed for each metadata feature against the relative abundances of all ASVs, controling for age, gender, and BMI. P-values from all independent metadata models were globally re-adjusted using the Benjamini‒Hochberg (BH) method to calculate the false discovery rate (FDR) across all the metadata-ASV pairs simultaneously. The data were filtered to include only metadata features and ASVs that maintained at least one significant association with FDR < 0.1. Unsupervised hierarchical clustering was performed using the hclust R function with Ward's method (ward.D2) and the maximum distance metric.

sec.title: Regression models
sec.p: For each lifestyle/diet metadata parameter Xi , we used linear regression (implemented by the OLS function in statsmodels 0.14.4) to regress the MHI ( Y ) using the following parameters: Y~Linear(Xi,Age,Gender,Medical_Index,Lifestyle_Index*) where Lifestyle_Index* is the lifestyle index calculated without including Xi (e.g., if Xi is “MEDAS-score”, Lifestyle_Index* is the log of the ratio of good/bad lifestyle parameters excluding “MEDAS-score”). Each regressed variable was scaled to mean = 0, std = 1 before regression. Regression was performed in Python, and significant coefficients were defined as coefficients with 95% confidence interval not containing 0. The required amount of each metadata category to increase the MHI was calculated by inverse-transforming each Xi and multiplying by the resulting regression coefficient, estimating an average intake of 2000 kcal per day.

sec.title: Lipidomics run and quantification
sec.p: 100 μL of serum samples were diluted with 900 μL of a 1:1 (v/v) methanol: butanol (Merck, Cat# 106035 and 34867, respectively). The samples were vortexed, centrifuged, and the clear lipid extracts were transferred into glass HPLC vials (Cat# 8010-0542, Agilent). Lipid profiling was conducted using a Vanquish Flex HPLC system coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 240 mass spectrometer (both from Thermo Fisher Scientific). Chromatographic separation was achieved on an Acclaim C30 column (100 × 2.1 mm, 3.0 µm; Thermo Fisher Scientific) maintained at 60 °C. The mobile phase consisted of: Solvent A: acetonitrile: water (60:40, v/v) with 10 mM ammonium formate and 0.1% formic acid for positive mode and acetonitrile: water (60:40, v/v) with 10 mM ammonium acetate and 0.1% acetic acid for negative mode. Solvent B: isopropanol: acetonitrile (90:10, v/v) with the same additives. Gradient elution was programmed as follows: 0–3 min: 30% B → 3–5 min: 43% B → 5–5.1 min: 55% B → 5.1–8 min: 60% B →8–18 min: 65% B → 18–24 min: 85% B → 24–26 min: 100% B → 26–33 min: 30% B. Samples were kept at 6 °C and injected in 5 µL volumes. The mass spectrometer was operated in both positive and negative-ion modes over an m/z range of 120–1,700. Full MS scans were acquired at a resolution of 120,000, and data-dependent MS/MS (dd-MS/MS) was performed using a 1.5-second cycle time and dynamic exclusion, with a normalized collision energy (NCE) of 30% and a resolution of 30,000. The scan range mode was set to ‘Define First Mass’. Lipid identification and annotation were carried out using LipidSearch™ 5.0 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The following search parameters were applied: precursor ion tolerance of 5 ppm, product ion tolerance of 5 ppm, product ion threshold of 5%, identification confidence levels A/B/C, retention time alignment deviation of 0.1 min, and filtering by top-ranked isomer peaks using the “New Filter” option. Lipids were annotated to the species level, and alignment was performed using the mean-based method. Integration of the signals was carried out by Skyline Daily (V. 25. 1.1.206) using the export option of LipidSearch™ output into a Skyline List. Lipid species showing relative standard deviation (RSD) >30% in pooled QC samples or >30% missing data across the dataset or signal-to-noise ratio below 5 were excluded from further analysis. Serum lipidomics datasets used in this study are provided in Dataset S2. For the lipidomics analyses, Spearman correlations were calculated between each lipid and each metadata category. Following Benjamini‒Hochberg FDR control, metadata categories with no significant correlations (q < 0.1) were removed, and features were clustered using single-linkage hierarchical clustering with a Euclidean distance metric. For lipid saturation analysis, a new feature X sample matrix was created by multiplying the (sample X lipid) frequency matrix with the (lipid X number of double bonds per lipid chain) matrix. Spearman correlation was then calculated between each new feature and each metadata category (and p-values were corrected using Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control).
